notes.meaning: Judah moved away from his father Jacob's household and went down to live near the Canaanite town of Adullam. There he became close friends with a local man named Hirah. Leaving the family of faith to make close ties among pagan neighbors put Judah in spiritual danger.

While living among the Canaanites, Judah saw the daughter of a local man named Shua and married her. Abraham and Isaac had warned their families against marrying Canaanite women, but Judah chose her without consulting his father. Mixing with the people of Canaan threatened the purity of the family God had chosen.
Judah's wife became pregnant and gave birth to their first son. Judah named the baby boy Er. This was the start of Judah's own household in the land.
Before long, Judah's wife had a second boy. This time she chose the baby's name and called him Onan. The name reflects sorrow or grief.

She gave birth to a third son named Shelah while staying at Chezib. Chezib was a town located in the low hills of Judah. Shelah would be the only one of these three original sons to survive to old age.

When Er grew up, Judah arranged a marriage for his firstborn son by finding a woman named Tamar. As the father and head of the household, Judah followed the custom of choosing his son's bride. Tamar joined Judah's family as the wife of the oldest heir.

Er lived in open defiance of the Lord and did what was evil in God's eyes. Because of his wickedness, God judged him and ended his life early. The Bible does not name his exact crime, but God saw it and punished him directly.

Judah directed Onan to marry Tamar under an ancient family custom known as levirate marriage. If a married man died without children, his brother was expected to marry the widow so their first child could carry on the dead brother's name and property. This duty protected the widow and kept the family line alive.

Onan took Tamar as his wife, but he knew any child they had would legally belong to Er rather than himself. Whenever they were together, he deliberately spilled his seed on the ground to prevent a pregnancy. He took the physical benefits of marriage while cheating his dead brother and Tamar out of an heir.

differ.view: Many evangelicals teach that Onan's sin was his greedy, selfish refusal to fulfill his family duty and provide an heir for his brother, not a blanket prohibition of birth control.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that God condemned Onan because using unnatural means to block the transmission of life within marital intimacy is intrinsically immoral.

notes.meaning: Onan's selfish and cruel act greatly displeased the Lord. Because Onan worked against his brother and refused his duty, God put him to death as well. God showed Himself as the holy judge over the hidden sins of the family.

differ.view: Onan was judged because of his selfish greed and his refusal to fulfill his family duty to raise up an heir for his brother, not because birth control itself is forbidden.
Onan's act of spilling his seed was a severe sin against the natural purpose of marriage and the gift of human life.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God struck Onan dead because he performed a deliberate contraceptive act that severed marital union from the procreation of life.

notes.meaning: Judah told Tamar to return to her father's home and live as a widow until young Shelah grew up. Secretly, Judah feared that Shelah might die just like his older brothers, so he blamed Tamar instead of his sons' wickedness. Tamar obeyed and returned home, but Judah left her bound to his family with no real intention of keeping his promise.

Years passed, and Judah's Canaanite wife died. After his period of mourning ended, Judah went up to Timnah with his friend Hirah to oversee the shearing of his sheep. Sheep-shearing was an annual festival season marked by feasting, drinking, and celebration.

Someone brought word to Tamar that her father-in-law was traveling up to Timnah for the shearing. She recognized that this journey offered a rare chance to confront the injustice done to her. Judah was away from home and celebrating with his workers.

Tamar saw that Shelah was fully grown, yet Judah had never given him to her as a husband. She took off her widow's mourning clothes, covered her face with a veil to hide her identity, and sat by the entrance to Enaim along the road to Timnah. She felt forced to take matters into her own hands to secure her rights in the family.

When Judah passed by, he mistook Tamar for a prostitute because her face was wrapped in a veil. Sitting alone by the roadside in disguise made her look like a woman offering herself for hire. Judah did not recognize his own daughter-in-law.

Judah turned aside from the main road, approached the disguised woman, and asked to sleep with her. He had no idea she was Tamar, and she immediately asked what payment he would give her. God allowed Judah's lust to blind his judgment so he did not even recognize her voice.

Judah promised to send her a young goat from his flock as payment for her services. Tamar agreed to the price, but she insisted that he leave a security deposit until the animal arrived. She was not after wealth, but wanted an unmistakable proof of who the man was.

When Judah asked what deposit she wanted, Tamar asked for his seal, the cord he wore around his neck, and his carved walking staff. In the ancient world, these items served like personal identification and carried his family authority. Judah gave them away to satisfy his lust, slept with her, and she became pregnant.

After Judah left, Tamar got up quickly and returned to her home. She took off the disguise and put her regular widow's clothing back on. Her quick departure showed that she was not living as a common prostitute, but had acted solely to obtain an heir.

Judah sent his friend Hirah with the promised young goat to redeem the personal items he had left behind. Hirah went to the spot where the encounter happened, but the woman was nowhere to be found. Judah wanted to handle the matter quietly through a friend to protect his reputation.

Hirah asked the local townsmen where to find the religious shrine prostitute who had been sitting by the roadside at Enaim. The Canaanites had women dedicated to pagan fertility shrines, but the locals told him that no such prostitute had ever been there. Hirah could find no trace of her.

Hirah returned to Judah and admitted that his search had failed completely. He told Judah that even the local people insisted there was no prostitute in that place. The mission had reached a dead end.

Judah told Hirah to let the woman keep his seal and staff so they would not become a public laughingstock. He had fulfilled his promise by sending the goat, and searching any further would only expose his shameful secret. Judah cared far more about what people thought of him than about God's opinion.

About three months later, neighbors noticed Tamar was pregnant and reported to Judah that his daughter-in-law had acted like a prostitute. Since she was legally promised to Shelah, Judah treated her pregnancy as adultery. Acting with the authority of a family patriarch, Judah angrily demanded that she be brought out and burned to death.

As she was being led out, Tamar sent the seal, cord, and staff to Judah with a quiet message asking him to examine them. She announced that she was pregnant by the man who owned those specific objects. Without causing a wild scene, she presented undeniable proof of the father's identity.

Judah recognized his personal belongings and confessed that Tamar was more righteous than he was. He admitted his deep failure in withholding his youngest son Shelah from her, which had provoked the whole crisis. He showed genuine repentance by leaving her alone and never sleeping with her again.
When Tamar went into labor, it became clear that twin boys were in her womb. God showed mercy to this broken family by replacing the two sons Judah had lost. A complicated birth was about to unfold.

During the labor, one baby reached his hand out first. The midwife quickly tied a bright scarlet thread around his wrist so everyone would know who was born first and had the rights of the oldest son. In ancient families, the birthright was of great importance.

The baby pulled his hand back into the womb, and his brother pushed ahead and was born first. The midwife was surprised at this sudden breakout and named the boy Perez, which means a breach or breaking through. This younger brother claimed the firstborn place, just as Jacob had done with Esau.

Soon afterward, the other twin was born with the scarlet thread still tied around his wrist, and he was named Zerah. Even though Zerah showed his hand first, it was Perez through whom the royal line of Judah continued. Through this unusual story of human failure and God's grace, Perez became an ancestor of King David and Jesus Christ.
